articles.title: California Will Allow Two Detached ADUs on Many Single-Family Lots: What LA Homeowners Should Know About AB 956
articles.body_html:
A newly signed California law could materially change how some Los Angeles homeowners think about their backyards.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 956 on September 29, 2026. Beginning January 1, 2027, the law increases the number of detached, newly constructed accessory dwelling units that local governments must ministerially approve on qualifying lots with an existing or proposed single-family home from one to two.

For Los Angeles homeowners and small investors, that is potentially significant.

It does not mean every property can suddenly support two backyard houses. Lot dimensions, fire access, utilities, building codes, height rules and other physical constraints still matter.

But the legal starting point is changing.

What does AB 956 actually change?

Under the signed legislation, a local agency must provide a ministerial pathway for two detached, new-construction ADUs on a lot with a proposed or existing single-family dwelling.

A local agency may impose a floor-area limit of no less than 800 square feet of livable space on each qualifying detached unit, along with applicable state height standards and side and rear setbacks of no more than four feet.

Ministerial approval is important because it generally means an application is reviewed against objective standards rather than going through a discretionary public-hearing process.

That can make the entitlement question more predictable. Construction itself is still another matter.

When does the new two-ADU rule begin?

AB 956 was signed September 29 and is expected to take effect January 1, 2027.

That date matters if you are considering a project now.

I would not assume that an application submitted under today's rules automatically receives the benefit of the new law before it becomes effective.

Anyone considering a project around the transition should verify the applicable filing rules with the local permitting agency and appropriate professionals.

Can every Los Angeles homeowner build two ADUs?

No.

State authorization is only one part of feasibility.

A property still has to physically accommodate the units.

I would want to evaluate lot width and depth, existing structures, setbacks, utility connections, sewer capacity, grading, fire access, trees, easements and the location of the existing house before assuming two units make sense.

A large flat lot with a house near the front can present a very different opportunity from a narrow hillside parcel where the existing house already consumes much of the buildable area.

Legal capacity and practical capacity are not the same thing.

Could each detached ADU be 800 square feet?

The new statute allows local agencies to impose a total floor-area limitation of not less than 800 square feet of livable space on qualifying detached ADUs under this pathway.

That creates an interesting planning question.

Two 800-square-foot units could potentially create 1,600 square feet of additional residential space on the right property.

But homeowners should not start with the maximum theoretical square footage. Start with the site.

Sometimes one well-designed larger unit may be more practical than two separate structures. On another property, two smaller units may make sense.

The best configuration depends on the lot and the owner's objective.

Can I build two detached ADUs plus a JADU?

Do not assume that you can.

AB 956 specifically says a local agency is not required to ministerially approve a junior accessory dwelling unit on a lot where two detached new-construction ADUs have been built.

That distinction is important because homeowners may see the new rule and begin adding every unit type allowed under different sections of ADU law.

The rules do not necessarily stack indefinitely.

Before designing a project around several unit types, confirm the exact combination permitted on the property.

Why could this matter so much in Los Angeles?

Land is expensive.

That means a large portion of a Los Angeles property's value can sit in the lot itself.

If state law allows a homeowner to create additional legal housing on land already owned, the economics can be very different from purchasing another parcel.

That does not mean an ADU is automatically profitable.

Construction costs, financing, utilities, insurance, taxes, maintenance, vacancy and achievable rent all have to be considered.

But the ability to spread land cost across additional units can create opportunities that would be difficult to reproduce through a separate acquisition.

Could two ADUs work as rentals?

Potentially.

State law requires rentals of ADUs created under this section to be for terms longer than 30 days.

For an investor-minded homeowner, the relevant calculation is therefore not simply: How much rent could two units produce?

I would calculate the total project cost, financing cost, realistic long-term rents, utilities, insurance, additional maintenance, reserves and expected vacancy.

Then compare the projected return with other uses of the capital.

An ADU can be a good project and still be a poor investment if construction costs become too high.

What about multigenerational housing?

Rental income is only one use.

Two detached units could create more flexibility for families who want aging parents, adult children or extended family nearby without placing everyone under one roof.

That may be particularly useful in Los Angeles, where buying several nearby properties can be prohibitively expensive.

An owner might eventually use one unit for family and another as a rental.

The ability to change uses over time can itself be valuable.

What does AB 956 change for HOAs?

AB 956 also changes language governing restrictions on ADUs in certain planned developments.

The law broadens protections from lots zoned for single-family residential use to lots zoned to allow single-family residential use. That can extend protection to additional properties where single-family housing is permitted even if the underlying zoning is not exclusively single-family.

This does not mean every condominium owner can automatically construct an ADU.

Common-interest-development rules and property configuration remain important.

Owners in an HOA should review the exact property type and governing documents before assuming the new law applies.

Could this affect property value?

Potential development capacity can matter to buyers.

A property with room for additional legal units may appeal to investors, multigenerational households or buyers who want future rental income.

But I would not simply add the projected construction cost or theoretical rental value to a home's asking price.

A buyer still has to spend money and take on construction risk to create those units.

The better approach is to evaluate ADU potential as one component of the property's overall value.

Should sellers build the ADUs before selling?

Not necessarily.

There are at least three possible strategies.

A seller could build and stabilize the units before selling. A seller could obtain plans or permits and market a more clearly defined development opportunity. Or the seller could simply market the property's potential and let the next owner undertake the project.

Which option produces the best result depends on construction cost, timing, available capital and the buyer pool.

Spending $400,000 on a project does not guarantee the eventual sale price rises by $400,000.

What should buyers do differently in 2027?

If you are shopping for a single-family property and ADU development is part of the plan, lot utility deserves more attention.

Two homes with similar interior square footage may have very different development potential.

I would look at the position of the existing house, driveway access, backyard dimensions, topography and neighboring improvements.

A beautiful backyard is one thing. A backyard that can efficiently support additional legal housing is something else.

Frequently asked questions

What is AB 956? AB 956 is a California housing law signed September 29, 2026 that expands the state's ministerial ADU rules.

How many detached ADUs will California require cities to allow? Beginning in 2027, qualifying single-family lots can receive ministerial approval for up to two detached new-construction ADUs under the applicable state pathway.

When does AB 956 take effect? January 1, 2027.

Can I automatically build two 800-square-foot ADUs? Not automatically. The state framework allows the units, but physical site conditions, applicable building standards and other requirements still determine whether a particular design works.

Can I also add a JADU? A city is not required to approve a JADU on the same lot once two detached new-construction ADUs have been constructed under this provision.

Is this legal or investment advice? No. Property owners should confirm the current rules for their specific parcel with the appropriate city agencies and qualified legal, design, construction and financial professionals.

Paul's take

This is the type of housing law that can change how I evaluate a property.

If two houses have similar living area and similar prices but one has a flat, usable rear yard with good access and the other does not, their future flexibility may be very different.

I would not buy a property solely because two ADUs might fit.

But if rental income, multigenerational living or long-term development potential is important to the buyer, AB 956 makes lot configuration even more relevant.

For Los Angeles buyers and owners, the backyard is increasingly something that should be analyzed alongside the house.

articles.title: Hotel Clark Finally Opens in Downtown Los Angeles: Inside a Decades-Long Adaptive Reuse Story
articles.body_html:
One of Downtown Los Angeles' strangest unfinished real-estate stories finally has an ending.

Hotel Clark has soft-opened at 426 S. Hill Street, bringing a long-dormant historic building back into active use with 348 guest rooms. The hotel is now accepting guests after an unusually long redevelopment history in which renovation work was largely completed years before the building actually opened.

For Downtown, the significance is not simply another hotel.

It is the reactivation of a large historic property that spent years sitting essentially finished but unused.

What is Hotel Clark?

Hotel Clark is an 11-story historic hotel on Hill Street in Downtown's Historic Core.

The current property contains 348 modernized rooms and sits near Pershing Square and several of Downtown's major civic, cultural and commercial destinations.

The building originally contained more than 500 guestrooms and dates to the early twentieth century.

Its history since then has been unusually complicated.

Why did Hotel Clark take so long to reopen?

The property went through decades of changing ownership, abandoned plans and redevelopment attempts.

At one point it was acquired by the People's Republic of China with plans for a business and cultural center. That proposal did not materialize.

Later redevelopment efforts converted the property back toward hotel use.

The unusual part is that much of the interior renovation was reportedly finished by 2014, yet the building remained closed for roughly another decade.

That makes the opening particularly interesting from a real-estate perspective. Construction completion does not necessarily mean a property has achieved economic activation.

What does the reopened hotel include?

In addition to 348 guestrooms, current property information describes more than 11,000 square feet of meeting and event space, a second-floor pool deck, on-site parking and multiple food-and-beverage concepts.

Its restaurant, Votana, is expected to have a larger opening celebration October 15.

The hotel is still in a soft-opening phase, which means operations and individual amenities may continue evolving.

That is worth remembering if you plan to visit immediately.

Why does adaptive reuse matter Downtown?

Downtown Los Angeles contains a large inventory of historic commercial buildings that would be extremely difficult to reproduce today.

Adaptive reuse gives some of those buildings a new economic purpose without erasing the architecture that makes them distinctive.

Hotels, apartments and other uses can sometimes work in buildings that no longer function competitively for their original purpose.

The process is not always easy. Older buildings can present structural, mechanical, accessibility and floor-plan challenges.

Hotel Clark demonstrates another risk: a redevelopment can consume enormous time and capital before the building produces income.

Why is the location interesting?

Hotel Clark sits on Hill Street near Pershing Square.

That places it within walking distance of portions of the Historic Core, Grand Central Market, Broadway, Bunker Hill and Downtown's civic center.

It also places the hotel near rail transit.

For a visitor, that creates a very different experience from staying at a freeway-oriented hotel.

The surrounding neighborhood becomes part of the stay.

What can a hotel add to a neighborhood?

Hotels create a rotating population of visitors.

Those visitors eat at restaurants, buy coffee, attend events, shop and use transportation.

A functioning 348-room property therefore has the potential to generate more street-level economic activity than an empty building.

That does not mean one hotel can solve Downtown's larger challenges. It cannot.

But active buildings are generally more useful to a neighborhood than dormant ones.

Does this mean Downtown Los Angeles is back?

I would avoid that framing.

Downtown is too large and complicated to describe through one opening.

Different districts have different conditions.

Office vacancy, homelessness, public safety, residential demand, tourism, transit and entertainment activity all interact differently across Downtown.

Hotel Clark reopening is a positive piece of information. It is not proof that every Downtown real-estate problem has been resolved.

That distinction matters when evaluating property.

What does this tell us about vacant buildings?

An empty building is not necessarily an easy redevelopment opportunity.

A property may look underused from the street while carrying substantial structural, legal, financing or operational complications.

That is particularly true with historic buildings.

For investors, the lesson is straightforward.

The purchase price is only the beginning. You need to understand what it will take to place the property into productive use.

Could the hotel help nearby businesses?

Potentially.

Hundreds of hotel rooms create a built-in customer base for food, entertainment and services.

Guests may visit Grand Central Market, nearby restaurants, museums, events and other Downtown destinations.

Meeting and event space can also bring visitors who are not staying overnight.

The economic effect will depend on occupancy and how guests actually use the surrounding neighborhood.

But converting a closed building into an occupied hotel creates opportunities that did not exist when the property was dark.

What about residential buyers Downtown?

I would not use the hotel opening as a reason by itself to purchase a condo.

Instead, I would treat it as another data point when evaluating the trajectory of the immediate area.

What businesses are opening? What buildings remain vacant? How does the block feel during the day and at night? How close is transit? What construction is underway? What are HOA finances and reserves in the building you are considering?

Neighborhood momentum matters, but the condominium itself still has to make sense.

Hotel Clark also illustrates the value of architecture

Los Angeles has historically been quick to demolish older buildings.

Adaptive reuse offers another option.

A historic building can retain the visual character of an older city while functioning for contemporary uses.

That can be especially valuable Downtown, where the mix of early twentieth-century architecture and newer towers creates a physical environment unlike most other Los Angeles neighborhoods.

The best adaptive-reuse projects do not simply preserve a facade. They give the building a reason to remain useful.

Frequently asked questions

Is Hotel Clark open? Yes. The property soft-opened in late September 2026 and is accepting reservations.

Where is Hotel Clark? 426 S. Hill Street in Downtown Los Angeles.

How many rooms does Hotel Clark have? 348 guestrooms.

What restaurant is at Hotel Clark? Votana is the property's Mediterranean-influenced restaurant and is expected to hold its larger opening celebration October 15.

Why is the opening notable? The historic property went through decades of redevelopment attempts and reportedly sat with much of its renovation completed for years before finally reopening.

Paul's take

I find Hotel Clark interesting because it shows how different real-estate timelines can be from what people expect.

From the street, a finished building can look like a project that simply needs someone to unlock the doors. The reality can be much more complicated.

Hotel Clark spent years representing unrealized potential. Now it is finally an operating property.

For Downtown, I think the most useful way to view the opening is not as evidence that the neighborhood has suddenly solved all of its problems. It is evidence that one more large, historic building has returned to productive use.

Those incremental changes are what I would continue watching.

articles.title: 303 For-Sale Homes Planned in Valley Village: What the Former ABC Radio Site Could Become
articles.body_html:
A large former broadcast property in Valley Village could become something Los Angeles does not build nearly as often as apartments: a substantial new community of for-sale homes.

Plans filed for the former ABC Radio property at 12755 Burbank Boulevard call for just over 303 homes across a 19-acre site. The proposal includes both traditional single-family houses and townhomes, with five percent of the homes reserved for lower-income purchasers.

That makes this project worth watching for buyers.

Much of Los Angeles' recent housing development has focused on rental apartments. This proposal is different.

What is proposed at 12755 Burbank Boulevard?

The current plan would redevelop a former ABC Radio broadcast facility into a low-rise residential community.

The proposal includes approximately 303 for-sale homes with a mixture of single-family houses and townhomes.

Floor plans are expected to range from one to five bedrooms.

Buildings would reach up to three stories, and the development would include parking for 727 vehicles.

That combination gives the project a substantially different character from the podium apartment buildings appearing along many Los Angeles commercial corridors.

How large is the site?

Approximately 19 acres.

That scale matters.

Many Los Angeles housing developments are assembled from one or several relatively small parcels.

A 19-acre site gives a developer room to think about streets, landscaping, open space and the relationship between buildings rather than fitting one structure onto a constrained urban lot.

The site reportedly sold for more than $70 million in 2025.

Will these be rentals?

The proposal is for for-sale housing, which is one of the reasons I think it deserves attention.

Los Angeles needs rental housing, but ownership inventory matters too.

A household deciding between a condominium, townhome and detached house has very different options from a renter choosing between apartment buildings.

Adding hundreds of new ownership units in one development could create a meaningful new option for Valley buyers if the project ultimately proceeds as proposed.

What types of homes are planned?

The developer is proposing both traditional single-family houses and townhomes.

That could allow the community to serve several buyer profiles.

A smaller townhome may appeal to a first-time buyer or someone who wants lower maintenance.

A larger detached home may appeal to a household that needs more bedrooms or private outdoor space.

The reported one-to-five-bedroom range suggests the project is not designed around a single household type.

Will there be affordable homes?

Yes, under the current proposal.

Five percent of the homes would be reserved for purchase by lower-income households as part of the project's density-bonus strategy.

The project still requires relevant approvals, so details can change before construction.

That is why I would describe these numbers as proposed rather than final.

What else is included?

Plans also call for publicly accessible green space and streetscape improvements along Burbank Boulevard.

That matters because a development of this scale is effectively creating a small neighborhood within a neighborhood.

The quality of streets, landscaping, sidewalks and common areas can materially affect how the finished community feels.

For a buyer, I would eventually want to understand not just the floor plan of an individual home, but the entire site plan.

Why does for-sale construction matter?

New ownership housing can be difficult to produce in Los Angeles.

Developers have to consider land, construction costs, financing, insurance, entitlement risk and the price buyers can actually afford.

Rental developments can sometimes be financed and operated under a different economic model.

That is one reason large apartment buildings are much more common in current Los Angeles development coverage than projects containing hundreds of individually owned homes.

A 303-home ownership community therefore stands out.

Could new construction help first-time buyers?

Potentially, but new does not necessarily mean inexpensive.

Pricing has not been established in the current public proposal.

New construction can command a premium because buyers receive modern systems, contemporary layouts and less immediate maintenance.

Townhomes can sometimes offer a lower entry point than detached houses, but that depends on size, location, HOA costs and final pricing.

I would wait for actual prices before describing the project as an affordability solution for market-rate buyers.

What should buyers eventually investigate?

If these homes reach the market, I would look beyond the base purchase price.

For attached or common-interest housing, buyers should understand HOA dues, what those dues cover, reserves, insurance and maintenance responsibilities.

For new construction, I would also want to understand builder warranties, upgrade pricing, property taxes, any special assessments or community facilities obligations, parking and future development phases.

A model home is designed to sell the lifestyle. The documents tell you what you are actually buying.

Could 303 new homes affect existing Valley Village sellers?

Possibly, particularly once the project begins selling.

New construction becomes another comparable option for buyers.

An existing townhome seller may eventually compete with brand-new townhomes nearby.

But existing homes can have advantages too. They may offer larger lots, established landscaping, lower HOA costs, different architecture or a better price per square foot.

Competition does not mean existing housing becomes obsolete. It means sellers need to understand what buyers can purchase elsewhere for similar money.

What could the project mean for Valley Village?

A 19-acre redevelopment is large enough to change the immediate area.

Hundreds of households create demand for nearby restaurants, grocery stores and services.

Public open space can create a neighborhood amenity. Streetscape improvements can change the experience along Burbank Boulevard.

There can also be additional traffic and pressure on surrounding infrastructure.

The appropriate question is not whether development creates change. It clearly does. The question is how the project is designed and how well that design integrates with the surrounding neighborhood.

Is construction starting now?

No.

The filing is an important step, but the proposal still requires approvals, including density-bonus incentives from the Los Angeles City Planning Commission.

That means this article should be treated as a description of the current proposal, not a guarantee that every detail will be built exactly as shown.

The next meaningful editorial milestone would be project approval, a major redesign, construction financing, groundbreaking or sales launch.

Why I would watch this project differently from another apartment building

Ownership changes the story.

If a 300-unit rental building opens, the immediate market question is usually rents and rental supply.

If 303 new homes go on sale, they become direct alternatives for buyers comparing existing houses, condominiums and townhomes throughout the eastern San Fernando Valley.

That creates a different competitive dynamic.

It also gives us actual transaction data once sales begin.

Eventually, we will be able to compare new-construction pricing with existing Valley Village inventory. That will be much more informative than renderings.

Frequently asked questions

How many homes are planned at the former ABC Radio property? Just over 303 for-sale homes are currently proposed.

Where is the project? 12755 Burbank Boulevard in Valley Village.

Are these apartments? No. Current plans call for for-sale single-family homes and townhomes.

How large is the property? Approximately 19 acres.

Will any homes be affordable? The proposal reserves five percent of the new homes for purchase by lower-income households.

When will the homes go on sale? A sales date has not been established. The project still requires approvals.

Paul's take

I think this is one of the more interesting housing proposals to come out this week because it adds something different to the conversation.

Los Angeles development news is frequently about apartments.

Here, we are talking about more than 300 potential ownership opportunities ranging from townhomes to larger houses.

I would not judge the project until we know final approvals, HOA structure and pricing.

But for buyers considering Valley Village and the surrounding Valley neighborhoods, this is absolutely a project I would keep on the radar.

Once pricing is available, the useful question will become very practical: how does a brand-new home here compare with what the same buyer can purchase in the existing resale market?
